extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners preparing/responding to Office actions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making and formatting nonstatutory double patenting rejections (including provisional rejections, use of secondary references, equitable bases, two‑way distinctness tests, and related form paragraphs) when examining U.S. patent applications under pre‑AIA and AIA rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection (no secondary references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claim [2] of copending Application No. [3] (reference application). Although the claims at issue are not identical, they are not patentably distinct from each other because [4]. This is a provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection because the patentably indistinct claims have not in fact been patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the patentably indistinct claims are in another copending application. Form paragraph 8.33 must precede this form paragraph and be used only once in an Office action. Do not use this paragraph if the patentably indistinct claims are in a patent (use 8.33 + 8.34 instead). May be used where reference application and application under examination: (a) name same inventive entity; (b) name different inventive entities but are commonly assigned; (c) are not commonly assigned but have at least one common (joint) inventor (unless confidentiality under 35 U.S.C. 122 prevents disclosure); (d) are filed by a common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118); (e) claim patentably indistinct inventions made within a joint research agreement scope under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (for pre‑AIA filings); or (f) claim patentably indistinct inventions and were commonly owned or deemed commonly owned under certain 35 U.S.C. provisions (for FITF/AIA). If the reference application is currently commonly assigned but file does not establish common ownership at time of invention, form paragraph 8.28.fti may be used additionally to resolve priority issues under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f)/(g). In bracket 4 provide appropriate explanation for anticipation or rationale for obviousness of the claims being rejected over the claims of the cited application. For pre‑AIA first‑to‑invent law, if the reference application is prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), also consider making a provisional 102(e)/103(a) rejection using form paragraph 7.21.01.fti; do not make/maintain such rejections if the reference application is disqualified as prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c). For FITF/AIA examinations, also make rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or 35 U.S.C. 103 where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting rejection with secondary reference(s) (primary reference = patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected on the ground of nonstatutory obviousness‑type double patenting as being unpatentable over claim [2] of U.S. Patent No. [3] in view of [4]. [5]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the primary reference is a patent that includes claims patentably indistinct from those in the application under examination (form paragraph 8.36). Form paragraph 8.33 must precede. In bracket 3 insert the number of the primary reference patent; in bracket 4 insert the secondary reference, which must be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 (or pre‑AIA 102 as applicable); in bracket 5 insert an explanation of the obviousness analysis. A provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection should also be made in the reference application. Additionally, make a rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) using form paragraph 7.21.fti if evidence indicates the primary reference patent is prior art under pre‑AIA 102(f) or (g) (e.g., applicant named prior inventor via form paragraph 8.28.fti) and the primary patent has not been disqualified under pre‑AIA 103(c). For pre‑AIA first‑to‑invent law, if primary patent is prior art under pre‑AIA 102(e), consider rejection under pre‑AIA 102(e)/103(a) using form paragraph 7.21.02.fti; do not maintain if disqualified under 103(c). For FITF/AIA, also consider rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or 35 U.S.C. 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection with secondary references (primary reference = copending application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claim [2] of copending Application No. [3] in view of [4]. [5] This is a provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use where the primary reference is a copending application and an obviousness analysis is required (form paragraph 8.37). Form paragraph 8.33 must precede. Do not use if patentably indistinct claims are in a patent (use 8.36 instead). May be used where copending application and application under examination: (a) name same inventive entity; (b) are commonly assigned; (c) not commonly assigned but have at least one common (joint) inventor (unless disclosure would violate 35 U.S.C. 122 confidentiality); (d) filed by common applicant (35 U.S.C. 118); (e) claim indistinct inventions under joint research agreement scope (pre‑AIA 103(c)); or (f) claim indistinct inventions and were commonly owned or deemed commonly owned under applicable provisions for FITF/AIA. If currently commonly assigned but file does not establish common ownership at time of later invention, use form paragraph 8.28.fti in addition to resolve priority issues under pre‑AIA 102(f)/(g). For FITF/AIA, if primary reference application is to a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned, also use form paragraph 8.28.aia if no evidence of common ownership not later than the effective filing date; make 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or 103 rejections where appropriate. In bracket 3 insert number of primary reference application; bracket 4 insert secondary reference (must be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102); bracket 5 insert explanation of obviousness analysis. Provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection should also be made in the primary reference application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph usage and ordering (8.33–8.39)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 8.33 must precede any one of form paragraphs 8.34 to 8.39 and must be used only ONCE in an Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the appropriate follow‑on form paragraph based on whether the patentably indistinct claims are in another application or in a patent and whether secondary references are involved. Use 8.35/8.37 for provisional rejections (copending application primary) without/with secondary references; use 8.36 when primary is a patent with secondary references. Use form paragraphs 8.38 and 8.39 when the basis for nonstatutory double patenting rejection is equitable principles (Schneller) — only with TC Director approval (see Schneller guidance). Always ensure 8.33 precedes and is used only once per Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional rejection under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) when reference is prior art under 102(f) or 102(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should additionally be made under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) using form paragraph 7.21.fti if: (a) evidence indicates that the reference patent/application is prior art under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g) (e.g., applicant has named the prior inventor in response to a requirement made using form paragraph 8.28.fti); and (b) the reference patent/application has not been disqualified as prior art in a pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection pursuant to pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this additional rejection where the facts support a 102(f)/(g) prior‑art determination and the reference has not been disqualified under 103(c). For pre‑AIA 102(e) references, use appropriate 102(e)/103(a) form paragraphs (7.21.01.fti or 7.21.02.fti) as described elsewhere; do not maintain such rejections if the reference is disqualified under 103(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply FITF/AIA statutory equivalents where appropriate (35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) / 35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications being examined under the first inventor to file (FITF) provisions of the AIA: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or 35 U.S.C. 103 should also be made if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining under AIA/FITF rules, convert/prefer AIA statutory grounds (e.g., 102(a)(2)) where facts indicate a patent or application constitutes prior art under AIA standards. Also follow FITF‑specific form paragraph guidance (e.g., 8.28.aia) when addressing common ownership questions absent evidence of common ownership not later than the effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑way test for distinctness (when required and how to apply)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two‑way test is to be applied only when the applicant could not have filed the claims in a single application and the Office is solely responsible for any delays. When making a two‑way distinctness determination, apply the obviousness analysis twice: (1) analyze obviousness of the application claims in view of the patent claims; and (2) analyze obviousness of the patent claims in view of the application claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both analyses lead to a conclusion that the claimed invention is an obvious variation of the invention claimed in the other application/patent, an obviousness‑type nonstatutory double patenting rejection is appropriate. If either analysis does not lead to a conclusion of obviousness, no obviousness‑type double patenting rejection is made (though equitable double patenting may still be possible). Unless the record clearly shows administrative delay solely caused by the Office and that the applicant could not have avoided separate filings, the examiner may use the one‑way distinctness determination and shift the burden to the applicant to show why a two‑way determination is required. The MPEP cites case law (In re Berg; In re Hubbell; In re Goodman; Pierce v. DuMont; In re Emert; In re Braat) illustrating factors: applicant control of prosecution, applicant delay (e.g., repeated extensions, abandonments and continuations), or Office delay. Document reasons for adopting one‑way vs two‑way approach and apply both directions only when warranted by facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting rejection based on equitable principles (Schneller / Geneva)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some circumstances a nonstatutory double patenting rejection is applicable based on equitable principles to prevent unjustified timewise extension of patent rights — enforceable no matter how the extension is brought about (examples: In re Schneller; Geneva Pharmaceuticals v. GlaxoSmithKline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schneller‑type equitable rejections are rare and require approval of the Technology Center (TC) Director before being made. Examiner should first consult with their Supervisory Patent Examiner (SPE); if SPE agrees, obtain TC Director approval. Use form paragraph 8.38 (between an issued patent and one or more applications) or 8.39 (provisional rejection between applications) for such rejections. The factual inquiry focuses on whether allowance of the later claims would improperly extend the right to exclude granted in an earlier patent and whether there was any apparent reason applicant was prevented from presenting the later claims during prosecution of the earlier application. Case examples (Schneller, Kaplan, Geneva) explain distinctions and limits: Schneller limited to facts of the case; Kaplan reversed double‑patenting where the patent disclosure was improperly treated as prior art and statutory filing constraints justified separate filings; Geneva applied equitable principles to invalidate later claims without an obviousness analysis where later claims merely claimed an earlier disclosed utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracket/fill‑in guidance for form paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert appropriate information into numbered brackets in form paragraphs: e.g., bracket 1 = claim number(s) being rejected; bracket 2 = claim number(s) of reference; bracket 3 = number of the reference patent or application; bracket 4 = explanation of subject matter or secondary reference; bracket 5 = explanation of obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the specific bracket guidance in each form paragraph: • For form paragraph 8.35/8.37 bracket 3 = number of reference application; bracket 4 = secondary reference (must be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102); bracket 5 = explanation of obviousness analysis. • For form paragraph 8.36 bracket 3 = number of primary reference patent; bracket 4 = secondary reference; bracket 5 = explanation of obviousness analysis. • For Schneller‑type paragraphs 8.38/8.39 bracket 4 = description of subject matter covered in the earlier patent/application. Ensure clarity in bracketed explanations to support anticipation or obviousness rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting in design/plant vs utility situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting issues may be raised where an applicant has filed both a utility patent application (35 U.S.C. 111) and either an application for a plant patent (35 U.S.C. 161) or a design patent (35 U.S.C. 171). In general, the same double patenting principles and criteria that are applied in utility‑utility situations are applied to utility‑plant or utility‑design situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double patenting rejections in utility‑plant situations may be made in appropriate circumstances. Double patenting is rare in design‑utility contexts; courts have found in some cases no double patenting where the utility claims are directed to internal construction and design claims to external appearance (Carman Indus. v. Wahl). Two‑way distinctness determinations may be necessary in design‑utility cases depending on facts. Apply case law and policy consistently and evaluate whether claims are directed to the same invention or obvious variations.
